SCORING_RULES: Consistent = earns the level. One good rep does not qualify.
Any single item on the failure list = level not met.
Speed or trail complexity can trigger any failure mode.
Assess under real trail conditions whenever possible.
Assess at start of every season — skills regress in off-season.

body_position.name: Body Position
body_position.description: Foundation for Braking and Cornering. Three accumulated steps: (1) standing ready appropriate to terrain, (2) BBS S/S and F/B, (3) pumping / pressure control.
body_position.calibration_note: Most student-athletes top out at Level 2. Level 3 is a realistic and meaningful goal for a full season of coaching. Level 4 is genuinely exceptional — fewer than a dozen riders in 12 seasons of IICL coaching have demonstrated it consistently. Level 5 represents elite skill beyond what NICA trails require.
notes: Weight shifts at Levels 1–2 are unintentional failures. At Levels 4–5, intentional F/B pressure control is correct execution — loading for features.

levels.2: Controlled setting. Sometimes on easy trail.
levels.3: Trail most of the time. Reverts when over-challenged.
levels.4: Always on trail across varied terrain. Largely autonomous — no conscious attention required.
levels.5: Bombproof. Fully autonomous. Tactical application of pressure control across all features. Beyond NICA trail scope.

levels.1: Knees pinch saddle or seated rather than standing ready. Rigid on bike. Looks at front wheel. 3 Key Essentials absent or inconsistent.
levels.2: Standing but rigid. Does not reliably adjust tall/low ready to terrain. Loses ready position with distraction or challenge. 3 Key Essentials fail with distraction.
levels.3: Standing ready appropriate to terrain most of the time. Tall/low selection mostly correct. 3 Key Essentials reliable. Reverts to stiff or close vision when significantly over-challenged.
levels.4: Always adjusts tall/low ready appropriately. 3 Key Essentials automatic. Never reverts.
levels.5: Low ready automatic under all conditions. Tactical adjustment to features.

levels.1: Absent. Rider static on bike. Weight shifts rigid and uncontrolled.
levels.2: Weight shifts forward or back unintentionally — from habit, misunderstanding, or fear. BBS F/B absent or minimal.
levels.3: BBS F/B present most of the time. Inconsistent on technical climbs or steep descents.
levels.4: BBS F/B always present. Intentional F/B loading for features — lunge on roll-down, step-up.
levels.5: Active F/B pressure control automatic. Foundation for front wheel lifts (OTB-201).

levels.2: BBS S/S absent or minimal. Rigidity prevents bike-body separation.
levels.3: BBS S/S present most of the time. Reverts on off-camber or through corners under pressure.
levels.4: BBS S/S always present. Spontaneous on trail across varied tread and camber.

levels.1: Absent. No awareness of tire loading.
levels.3: Emerging — intentional F/B loading beginning to appear on features. Inconsistent.
levels.4: Consistent intentional pressure control — loads features deliberately. Foundation for front wheel lifts (OTB-201).
levels.5: Full pumping / pressure control automatic. Foundation for wheelies and manuals (OTB-301). Beyond NICA trail scope.

1.detail: Knees pinch saddle or seated rather than standing ready. Rigid on bike — no BBS possible. Looks at front wheel. 3 Key Essentials absent or inconsistent: no deep bend in elbows and knees, elbows not wide, weight not in feet.

2.detail: Standing but rigid. Weight shifts forward or back unintentionally — from habit, misunderstanding, or fear. Does not reliably adjust tall/low ready to terrain. BBS S/S and F/B absent or minimal. 3 Key Essentials fail with distraction or challenge.

failure_modes: Pressure control only emerging on features
3.detail: Standing ready appropriate to terrain most of the time. Tall/low selection mostly correct. 3 Key Essentials reliable. BBS S/S and F/B present most of the time. Pressure control emerging — intentional F/B loading beginning to appear on features, inconsistent. Reverts to stiff or close vision only when significantly over-challenged.

4.detail: Always adjusts tall/low ready appropriately to terrain steepness and features. 3 Key Essentials automatic. BBS S/S and F/B always present. Intentional F/B loading for features — lunge on roll-down, step-up. Pressure control consistent. Foundation for front wheel lifts (OTB-201). Largely autonomous — no conscious attention required.

failure_modes: Full tactical pressure control any terrain
5.detail: Low ready automatic under all conditions. Full pumping / pressure control automatic across all features and terrain. Foundation for wheelies and manuals (OTB-301). Fully autonomous — tactical application. Beyond NICA trail scope.

braking.name: Braking
braking.description: Builds on standing ready position. Three accumulated steps: (1) both brakes with modulation, (2) bracing leg and hips back, (3) timing for corners and trail braking.
braking.calibration_note: Most student-athletes operate at Level 1–2. Reaching Level 3 is a meaningful seasonal goal. Level 4 requires significant experience and trail time.
notes: The Gary Test: an unexpected obstacle placed in the rider's path tests whether correct braking form survives surprise — the real measure of whether braking is internalized. Level 4 requires passing consistently on trail.

levels.2: Controlled setting with warning. Reverts in unexpected scenarios.
levels.3: Trail most of the time. Fails at extreme speed or most extreme surprise stops.
levels.4: Always solid on any trail terrain — planned and emergency stops. Largely autonomous.
levels.5: Any conditions. Tactical brake management. Beyond NICA trail scope.

levels.1: Rear brake only or heavily rear-biased. Two or three fingers on levers — no modulation possible. Grabs brakes resulting in skid. Afraid to brake hard — limited ability to slow down. Brakes in corners as default behavior.
levels.2: Even front/rear under perfect conditions. Unexpected stop yanks rear only — skids. Brakes in corners as panic response to speed or consequence.
levels.3: Good modulation — rarely skids. Powerful braking, short stopping distance. Consistent front/rear balance.
levels.4: Never skids. Both brakes always. Modulation fully consistent. Always brakes before corners.
levels.5: Precise modulation, timing, and intentional front/rear pressure for any conditions. Carries speed to last second before corner — brakes hard to precise entry speed. Senses traction loss in real time and modulates.

levels.1: Upper body shifts forward under hard braking. No weight management. Discomfort braking hard.
levels.2: Upper body shifts forward under unexpected stops. Some rearward shift in controlled stops.
levels.3: Hips back and down introduced — learning the movement. Present sometimes in normal stops. Not yet reliable under pressure or surprise.
levels.4: Hips back and down automatic in all stops including surprise situations.
levels.5: Full pressure control — releases front brake first, trails rear to settle suspension. Holds rear brake through steep corners to manage speed. Times braking to high-traction zones.

levels.2: Present in controlled expected stops. Lost in unexpected scenarios.
levels.3: Consistent except most extreme surprise stops.
levels.4: Always automatic — planned stops and emergency situations. Passes Gary Test consistently on trail.
levels.5: Maintained under all conditions including trail braking through corners.

1.detail: Rear brake only or heavily rear-biased. Two or three fingers on levers — no modulation possible. Grabs brakes resulting in skid. Afraid to brake hard — limited ability to slow down. Brakes in corners as default behavior.

2.detail: Even front/rear braking under perfect conditions. Unexpected stop yanks rear only — skids. Upper body shifts forward compounding the skid. Bracing leg present in controlled expected stops, lost in unexpected scenarios. Brakes in corners as panic response to speed or consequence.

failure_modes: Bracing leg lost at extreme surprise
Hips back and down: learning, not yet reliable
3.detail: Good modulation — rarely skids. Powerful braking, short stopping distance. Bracing leg consistent except most extreme surprise stops. Hips back and down introduced — learning the movement, present sometimes in normal stops, not yet reliable under pressure or surprise. Maintains body position enabling transition to cornering.

4.detail: Never skids. Both brakes always consistent. Braking always solid on any terrain — planned and emergency stops. Hips back and down automatic. Always braces leg including emergency situations. Brakes before corners consistently. Correct braking maintained in unexpected stops — passes Gary Test on trail.

5.detail: All foundational braking always correct. Precise modulation, timing, and intentional front/rear pressure for any conditions. Carries speed to last second before corner — brakes hard to precise entry speed — releases front first, trails rear to settle suspension. Holds rear brake through steep corners to manage speed. Senses traction loss on slippery surfaces and modulates in real time.

cornering.name: Cornering
cornering.description: Most extensive step progression. Sequence accumulates: Level 2: BBS S/S lean + maintains ready. Level 3: Low-Look-Lean + hip rotation/counterbalance. Level 4: Full sequence consistent. Level 5: Pumping / pressure control through apex.
cornering.calibration_note: Most student-athletes reach Level 2. Level 3 requires consistent BBS and introduction of hip rotation — a meaningful seasonal goal for athletes who train regularly.
notes: Panic is the consistency axis: weight back, braking in corner, squeezing bike and steering are common panic responses. Higher level = higher panic threshold.
Level 2 diagnostic: correct BBS S/S lean — inside elbow straightens, outside elbow bends acute, seat shifts toward inside thigh. Regress to BBS S/S drill if body-bike locked.

levels.1: Flat, predictable surface. Slow speed only.
levels.2: Controlled setting. Sometimes on easy trail with distinct corners.
levels.3: Easy trail most of the time. Reverts under higher speed or consequence.
levels.4: Always consistent on blue and black terrain. Largely autonomous. Panic rare.
levels.5: Any conditions. Fully autonomous. Panic essentially absent. Beyond NICA trail scope.

levels.1: Pedals uneven or inside pedal down. Seated — no ready position.
levels.2: Outside or inside pedal down. Seated or tall ready entering corner.
levels.3: Pedals level on entry most of the time. Low ready present but erodes mid-corner.
levels.4: Level pedals consistent. Low ready maintained through the arc always.
levels.5: Level pedals and low ready automatic under any conditions.

levels.1: No bike lean or leans to outside. Steers through all corners.
levels.2: Body and bike locked same lean — knees squeezed, no BBS S/S. Steers rather than leans. Eyes on threat rather than exit.
levels.3: BBS S/S lean consistent — correct direction, knees wide, elbows hinge, seat shifts toward inside thigh. Lean limited to OTB-101 range.
levels.4: BBS S/S lean always consistent. Lean angle appropriate to speed and corner. Eyes through exit consistently.
levels.5: BBS S/S maintained under all conditions.

levels.3: Present under ideal conditions — visibly greater lean than BBS alone. Absent under pressure.
levels.4: Always consistent on blue/black terrain. Lean angle reflects hip rotation throughout.
levels.5: Maintained under any conditions including high speed and varied tread.

levels.1: Weight too far forward or back — no awareness.
levels.2: Weight too far forward or back — from habit, misunderstanding, or fear. Both directions at this level.
levels.3: Weight generally centered. Loses fore/aft balance under pressure. Pressure control absent.
levels.4: Weight stable through arc. Pressure control present in ideal conditions — consistent banked corners.
levels.5: Pumps the apex — dynamic load through corner peak and mid-corner features. Momentum-dependent. Beyond NICA trail scope.

levels.1: Panic at low threshold — steers, brakes in corner, weight back.
levels.2: Panic at moderate speed — brakes in corner, weight back, squeezes bike and steers.
levels.3: Same panic pattern but higher threshold. Normal trail riding usually clean.
levels.4: Panic rare. Not present in normal trail riding. Recovers quickly.
levels.5: Panic essentially absent. Correct movement maintained under extreme speed and consequence.

1.detail: Setup: Pedals uneven or inside pedal down. Seated — no ready position. Lean: No bike lean or leans to outside. Steers through all corners. Eyes: On front tire or threat — increases perceived speed, triggers panic.

2.when_breaks: Breaks at faster or unpredictable corners
2.detail: Setup: Outside or inside pedal down. Seated or tall ready entering corner. Lean: Body and bike locked same lean — knees squeezed, no BBS S/S. May lean to outside. Steers rather than leans, especially under speed. Eyes: On front tire or threat rather than through exit. Panic: Braking in corner, weight back, squeezes bike and steers to compensate.

3.when_breaks: Breaks at higher speed or consequence
failure_modes: Hip rotation only in ideal conditions
3.detail: Setup: Pedals level on entry most of the time. Low ready present but erodes mid-corner. Lean: BBS S/S lean consistent — correct direction, knees wide, elbows hinge, seat shifts toward inside thigh. Lean limited to OTB-101 range. Hip: Hip rotation and counterbalance present under ideal conditions only. Eyes: Through exit most of the time. Reverts under pressure.

failure_modes: Hip rotation breaks at extreme consequence
Pressure control only on consistent banked corners
4.detail: Setup: Level pedals consistent. Low ready maintained through arc always. Lean: BBS S/S consistent. Hip: Hip rotation and counterbalance always consistent on blue/black terrain. Eyes: Through exit consistently. Rarely reverts. Weight: Stable through arc. Pressure control present under ideal conditions — consistent banked corners.

5.detail: Full sequence consistent under any conditions — rocky, off-camber, loose, rutted, drop exits. Pumps the apex: dynamic pressure load through corner peak maximises traction. Applied to mid-corner features (roots, rolls, drops). Momentum-dependent — cannot be held statically.

TRAIL_GUIDE.intro: Trail selection is a safety decision. It requires current skill assessment — not memory from last season, not an impression of fitness or speed, and not a single observation. Skills regress in the off-season. Every rider needs a current assessment before trail decisions are made for the season.
TRAIL_GUIDE.minimums_note: These are minimum skill levels to ride a trail class at trail speed. They are a floor, not a ceiling — a higher-rated rider can ride lower-rated trails. A lower-rated rider may ride short sections of higher-rated trails by managing speed or walking technical features.
TRAIL_GUIDE.trail_ratings_note: A trail's difficulty rating is earned by its hardest feature, not its average character. The coach's job: identify which specific feature type earns the trail its rating. Assess whether riders have the minimum skill for that feature. Set the minimum based on the feature, not just the trail rating.
assessment_rules: Assess during skills instruction, skills sessioning on trail, and while riding in normal conditions.
The rider must demonstrate the skill across varied conditions within the trail type — through corners, over water bars, at speed, on varied tread.
Provide correction until the target level is demonstrated reliably across multiple rides.
Any item on the failure list = level not met. Speed or trail complexity can trigger any failure mode.
TRAIL_GUIDE.real_example: A blue trail with features was selected for early-season riders based on a coach's memory that they were 'really good.' Skills were not assessed at the start of the season. Observed skill levels on trail: Body Position 1–2, Cornering 1. Minimum appropriate for this trail: Body Position 3, Cornering 2. One rider crashed. Stiff body position on a small feature was the direct cause. The rider was uninjured but the outcome was predictable from the assessment gap.
TRAIL_GUIDE.score_notation: Scores are expressed as Body Position – Braking – Cornering, e.g. 2-3-2.
score_examples: New rider at 1-1-1. Goal: reach 2-2-1 before first trail ride.
Ride group baseline: bring all athletes to 2-2-2 by start of in-season.
Varsity target: 3-3-3 to safely ride blue trails.
TRAIL_GUIDE.reassessment: Every two weeks on a consistent reference section exposing cornering, BBS, braking, and body position simultaneously.

COACH_NOTES.fitts_posner: The 1–5 scale maps directly to the three stages of motor learning described by Fitts and Posner, which NICA coach training covers. Levels 1–2 are the cognitive stage — movements are conscious, inconsistent, and fail under distraction. Level 3 is the associative stage — movements becoming reliable but breaking down under pressure. Level 4 is largely autonomous — foundational movements require no conscious attention, freeing the rider for terrain and tactics. Level 5 is fully autonomous with tactical application. Reaching Level 4 represents substantial skill development; reaching Level 5 is elite.
COACH_NOTES.calibration: Most student-athletes operate at Level 1–2. This is not a failure — it reflects the reality of developing athletes with limited trail time. Progress from Level 1 to Level 2 is a meaningful achievement worth recognizing. Level 3 is a realistic goal for athletes who train consistently across a full season. Level 4 is genuinely exceptional — fewer than a dozen riders across 12 seasons of IICL coaching have demonstrated it consistently. Level 5 represents elite skill that exceeds what NICA trails require.
common_errors: Confusing fitness with skill. A strong climber who steers corners is Level 1 in cornering.
Scoring best performance rather than consistent performance. 'Most of the time' earns Level 3, not Level 4.
Assessing on flat terrain only — most skills collapse on steeper or rougher ground.
Treating Level 4–5 as synonymous with 'fast.' Speed is not a criterion.
Using last season's assessment. Skills regress in the off-season. Assess at the start of every season.
interdependencies: Braking Level 3 requires Body Position Level 2 or higher.
Cornering Level 3 requires Body Position Level 2 and Braking Level 2.
At Levels 1–2, weight shifts are failures. At Levels 4–5 intentional F/B pressure control is correct execution.
key_essentials: Finger on each brake lever at all times
